entries.title: Injury-ridden Blackhawks ride Spencer Knight to fourth consecutive win
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>’ only viable formula to beat the Rangers on Friday was obvious well before the puck dropped.</p><p>With a lineup <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/27/blackhawks-patrick-kane-injury-update-bowen-byram-connor-bedard" target="_blank" >decimated by injuries</a>, they needed to find some offense from unlikely sources and rely on surging goalie Spencer Knight to tip the scale.</p><p>That’s exactly how it played out. The Hawks earned their fourth consecutive victory by grinding out a 2-1 decision in front of a season-high sellout crowd of 20,302 at the United Center.</p><p>They did it with only 10 shots on goal, their fewest in a regular-season game since the NHL began tracking that stat in 1959. The only previous instance came in a 1974 playoff victory against the Kings.</p><p>The Rangers, meanwhile, fired 31 shots on Knight, but only one shot beat him — and none did in the final two periods.</p><p>Knight has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/24/blackhawks-spencer-knight-warning-odd-man-rushes-workload" target="_blank" >found his A-game</a> in the last few weeks, going 5-1-1 with a .922 save percentage in his last seven starts. His plus-6.3 goals saved above average during that span ranks second-best in the league, trailing only Islanders star Ilya Sorokin.</p><p>‘‘We did a pretty good job of bending and not breaking,’’ coach Jeff Blashill said. ‘‘We had a lot of blocks. We defended hard around the net.</p><p>‘‘[We’re] not giving up some of the super-A-quality chances we were earlier in the year. You’re giving up more contested stuff. That’s the way you have to do it to give your goalie a chance to be great, and he was great.’’</p><p>Knight mentioned the Hawks’ long flight home from Seattle on Thanksgiving — which prevented them from practicing the day before a matinee, like usual — might have handicapped their performance, but it clearly didn’t handicap his.</p><p>‘‘People sometimes evaluate goaltending just based on results, but I think there’s a lot of times you can find good or bad in good or bad games,’’ Knight said. ‘‘There’s things I did wrong today. There’s things I did really well in the games I’ve given up four.’’</p><p>Andrew Mangiapane provided all the Hawks’ production with two power-play goals in the first period. Both times, he slipped unnoticed into the right side of the slot and, after taking passes from Oliver Moore and Ryan Donato, got the puck off his quickly.</p><p>Mangiapane certainly counts as an unlikely source of offense. Although he’s a relentless forechecker, he entered the day with zero goals in 12 games and had received zero seconds of ice time on the power play.</p><p>‘‘[It was] a little bit of a shock when I came in this morning and saw I was on the power play,’’ Mangiapane said. ‘‘[I] felt good, though.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Donato to Andrew Mangiapane who has his second power-play goal of the period. <a href="https://t.co/zAtUeRftpm">pic.twitter.com/zAtUeRftpm</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2126455462757310502?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 27, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Hawks, already missing three of their top six scorers, finally dodged one injury bullet. Top scorer Roman Kantserov left during the second period with an apparent hand or wrist issue but returned unaffected for the third.</p><p>Even with Kantserov, it will be difficult to cook with this recipe very often. Talent matters in this league, even if it can be overcome on a day-to-day basis, and the Wild will pose an especially tough challenge Sunday.</p><p>Among the forwards, the Hawks will need Frank Nazar and Moore to remain productive without Patrick Kane, need Anton Frondell to find a rhythm again and need more from Ryan Greene, who struggled Friday and doesn’t have a point since Halloween.</p><p>Blashill seems encouraged, however, that the Hawks are executing their system more consistently and developing more of a ‘‘smart pressure’’ style without being reckless.</p><p>‘‘There’s still more room for us to grow and play with the puck and make [more] plays,’’ Mangiapane said. ‘‘But you can see, from where we were at the start of the year to now, we’re winning more puck battles. Our compete level is what’s helping us win these games.’’</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Elite talents Grant Bowen, Jakobe Baldwin lead IC Catholic to 3A state title
entries.summary: <p>Grant Bowen has spent his entire life around IC Catholic football. His dad, Matt Bowen, played in the NFL and now serves as an assistant coach with the Knights.</p><p>“It’s surreal, being here six years ago as a little child and seeing [IC Catholic win state] in 2022 and then being here now winning it,” Grant Bowen said after the Knights knocked off St. Joseph-Ogden 61-26 in the Class 3A state title game on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/11/26/illinois-high-school-football-state-championship-scores-ihsa" >Friday</a> at ISU’s Hancock Stadium.</p><p>But that story happens every year in Illinois high school sports. It’s not uncommon to see a coach’s kid who watched a successful team grow up and eventually win his own high school title.</p><p>Bowen, a 6-4, 220-pound tight end, is not your typical coach’s kid. The junior is one of the country's top prospects, with more than 30 college scholarship offers.</p><p>That talent showed up nearly every time Bowen touched the ball. He caught four passes, and three went for touchdowns, all from more than 30 yards out.</p><p>And Bowen isn’t IC Catholic’s only elite talent. Running back Jakobe Baldwin is one of the state’s best sophomores. He had 20 carries for 335 yards and four touchdowns.</p><p>“Our offense is like a Swiss Army knife,” Bowen said. “We can do everything.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Bears fans told us what made Revie Sorey more than just an offensive lineman. 'Awesome human'
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Sun-Times readers shared memories of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/27/revie-sorey-bears-guard-blocked-walter-payton-dedicated-life-helping-at-risk-kids-dies-73" target="_blank" >late Chicago Bears offensive lineman Revie Sorey</a>, who helped pave the way for legendary running back Walter Payton. Here is what you told us, lightly edited. </p><p>"I got to meet him at an all-day charity event when I was a kid. The first Chicago Bears player I ever met in person. He was great to us that day, and I'll never forget shaking his hand. Rest easy, sir."<br><i>— Jerry LaBuy</i></p><p>"Lucky enough to meet this awesome human during his playing days. He couldn’t have been nicer to me or all the other fans that day. Rest easy, big fella."<br><i>— Steve Medel Sr.</i></p><p>"Classic player; what a thrill to watch him and Noah Jackson pave the way for Walter (Payton). Prayers."<br>— <i>Philip Doherty</i></p><p>"I was fortunate to work for him at the Hammond Boys & Girls Club. He became a great mentor of mine, and he has always held a special place in my heart. It’s a sad day in my home."<br><i>— Cathie Dull</i></p><p>"He and Noah Jackson came to my elementary school for an assembly. I can’t remember the purpose of the assembly, but the two put on a spectacular display of dunking basketballs on the 8-foot rims."<br><i>— Chris Zima</i></p><p>"I remember meeting him in grade school. He was a down-to-earth guy and was in tune with all of us youngsters." Prayers to his family.'<br><i>— Chris J Vieweg</i></p><p>"Revie’s racquetball tournaments were some of the largest racquetball tournaments played in Illinois. I was fortunate to play with him and against him in a few tournaments. My son also went to Revie's football camps. Rest in peace, Revie."<br>— <i>Patrice Marie</i></p><p>"Just saw this. Linemen for life. He and Noah Jackson were part of our childhood in the 70s."<br><i>— Steven Henkel</i><br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times staff
